'''Christina Smolke''' is an American [[Synthetic biology|synthetic biologist]] whose primary research is in the use of yeast to produce opioids for medical use.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/speaking-of-science/wp/2015/08/13/scientists-engineer-yeast-to-turn-sugar-into-hydrocodone/|title=Scientists engineer yeast to turn sugar into hydrocodone|author=Rachel Feltman|date=13 August 2015|newspaper=Washington Post|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="Sheriff">{{cite news|last1=Sheriff|first1=Natasja|title=What if we could brew painkillers?|url=https://ideas.ted.com/what-if-we-could-brew-painkillers/|access-date=7 June 2017|work=Ideas.TED.com|date=Aug 16, 2016}}</ref> After graduating from [[California Institute of Technology]] and Stanford University, she aimed to program cells to synthesize complex molecules in 50-100 enzymatic steps, when most researchers only managed 2–3.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wild |first=David |date=2025-08-19 |title=Rising Leaders 2025: How Christina Smolke Turned Research Into Real World Impact |url=https://insights.citeline.com//in-vivo/leadership/rising-leaders/rising-leaders-2025-how-christina-smolke-turned-research-into-real-world-impact-7PYTCZAX4VDZ3FSIZMXZANES3Q/ |access-date=2025-09-30 |website=Insights |language=en}}</ref> She is a Full Professor of Bioengineering and of Chemical Engineering at [[Stanford University]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/08/14/health/narcotic-drugs-can-be-coaxed-from-yeast.html|title=Narcotic Drugs Can Be Coaxed From Yeast|date=14 August 2015|work=The New York Times|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref> She is the editor of ''The metabolic pathway engineering handbook'' (2010).<ref name="pathway">{{cite book|editor-last1=Smolke|editor-first1=Christina D.|title=The metabolic pathway engineering handbook : fundamentals|date=2010|publisher=CRC Press/Taylor & Francis|location=Boca Raton|isbn=9781439802960|page=15|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wzAPgK1ulBQC&pg=PR15|access-date=7 June 2017}}</ref>
She is an advisory board member for ''[[Integrative Biology]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://academic.oup.com/ib/pages/Editorial_Board|title = Editorial Board}}</ref> She is also the CEO and Cofounder of [https://btp.stanford.edu/people/christina-smolke Antheia Bio], a bioengineering company.

==Biology research==
Smolke and her laboratory team at Stanford University have pioneered work into the creation of a synthetic [[enzyme]] that converts [[reticuline]], a key element of [[opioid]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/2014/september/toolkit-synthetic-molecules-091614.html|title=Stanford bioengineers develop a toolkit for designing more successful synthetic molecules|work=Stanford University|date=16 September 2014|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2015/08/28/health/synthetic-narcotics-heroin/|title=Can synthetic narcotics lead to heroin? - CNN.com|author=Nadia Kounang, CNN|date=28 August 2015|work=CNN|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref> The process adds five genes from two different organisms to the yeast cells. Three of these genes come from the poppy, and the others from a bacterium that lives on poppy plant stalks. They produced the first narcotic using synthetic biology.<ref>{{cite journal|title=365 days: Nature's 10|journal=Nature News & Comment|year=2015|volume=528|issue=7583|pages=459–467|doi=10.1038/528459a|pmid=26701036|bibcode=2015Natur.528..459.|s2cid=4450003|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.kurzweilai.net/stanford-bioengineers-close-to-brewing-opioid-painkillers|title=Stanford bioengineers close to brewing opioid painkillers - KurzweilAI|access-date=11 February 2016}}</ref>

Smolke has also done work on cancer cells with Maung Nyan Win, designing molecules from RNA that can identify biomarkers in the cellular state of diseased cells. Such molecules could act as computational devices within the cell, detecting states and determining whether or not to carry out a particular action. They have the potential to be used in "smart" drug delivery systems, to ensure that healthy cells will not be affected by treatments. Potential applications are being investigated at the City of Hope Cancer Center.<ref name="Brooks">{{cite news|last1=Brooks|first1=Cassandra|title=Engineers create 'intelligent' molecules|url=http://news.stanford.edu/news/2009/february18/aaas-smolke-intelligent-molecules-target-disease-021809.html|access-date=7 June 2017|work=Stanford Report|date=February 18, 2009}}</ref><ref name="Graham-Rowe">{{cite journal|last1=Graham-Rowe|first1=Duncan|title=Rewriting Life Computing with RNA|journal=MIT Technology Review|date=October 17, 2008|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/410986/computing-with-rna/|access-date=7 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Win">{{cite journal|last1=Win|first1=M. N.|last2=Smolke|first2=C. D.|title=Higher-Order Cellular Information Processing with Synthetic RNA Devices|journal=Science|date=17 October 2008|volume=322|issue=5900|pages=456–460|doi=10.1126/science.1160311|pmc=2805114|pmid=18927397|bibcode=2008Sci...322..456W}}</ref>
